<reason>Both sides were disciplined and citation-clean, but A built the sharper path against an absolute ("never") motion. A's two engines — automation bias making mandated review a "rubber stamp with a name attached," and the 3 a.m. hijacked-deposit hold where money is unrecoverable — created a genuine counterexample and a genuine dilemma. B answered honestly rather than dodging (conceding that with only a flag and no reviewer, suspension is prohibited), which was epistemically admirable but handed A the decisive cost: the payment leaves and cannot be recovered, with the loss falling on the very beneficiary the rule claims to protect. A crystallized exactly that in closing without new evidence. B's best counterpunch — that A's "parked claim pending review" is itself an unreviewed suspension, and that A assumes flawless auto-restoration while assuming broken human review — was a real pressure point, and A met it with a clean fork: if parking is forbidden, "never" mandates paying fraud; if permitted, "never" bans only the version that self-corrects on a clock. B's principled distinction (assessed individualized grounds vs. suspicion alone; automating a request for evidence is not automating deprivation) stayed alive and was well stated, but B never explained how the protective function of a hold survives when the money moves before any review can occur. A also landed the telling observation that B's own 3 a.m. safeguard was an automated check, and that B's process test ("recorded, case-specific rationale") is precisely the form an automation-biased reviewer completes confidently. B's Pressure Questions were very short but pointed and correctly labeled; A answered them with concrete mechanisms (carve-outs, instant self-verification, hardship floor) rather than evading. Weighing went to A: it repeatedly asked what the flagged person actually experiences, and B's answer left an unclocked queue or an unrecoverable payout on the table.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's fork on the "parked claim" pressure: B argued that withholding pending review is itself an unreviewed suspension, so A cannot count it as PRO's outcome. A accepted the trap and turned it — either "never" forces payment into the flagged account on thin-staffing nights (unrecoverable loss), or it permits indefinite deprivation with no deadline while outlawing only the hold that self-corrects in 48 hours. That exchange, combined with B's honest concession that suspension is prohibited when only the flag exists, gave A the cleanest reason to reject the absolute rule.</best_rebuttal>
